title: The Memory He Offers
subtitle: After Always · Chapter 24 of 40
content:
Snape gave me a memory on a Sunday afternoon.

No warning.

No explanation.

He placed a small glass vial beside my hand while I was updating the final audit index.

Silver mist moved inside it.

I stopped writing.

“What is this?”

“A memory.”

“I gathered that.”

“Then your question was unnecessary.”

I looked at him.

His face was pale but composed.

“Yours?”

“Yes.”

“Why are you giving it to me?”

“Because you keep asking questions.”

“I can stop.”

“That would be miraculous.”

“Snape.”

He looked toward the office.

“There are things I am unwilling to explain twice.”

The phrasing bothered me.

“Twice?”

“Once to you. Again at the hearing.”

I understood.

“This is evidence?”

“Partly.”

“Then why me?”

His eyes returned to mine.

“Because I would prefer one person in that room to know what it costs before it is shown.”

The hearing.

Harry's testimony would include selected memories if the Wizengamot requested corroboration. Snape had fought the idea for weeks.

Now he was offering me one first.

I did not touch the vial.

“Are you sure?”

“No.”

The honesty made my chest ache.

“Do you still want me to watch it?”

“Yes.”

“Will you be there?”

“Yes.”

Only then did I pick it up.

We used the Pensieve in McGonagall's office because Snape refused to keep one in the dungeon.

She left us alone.

The silver surface rippled.

Snape stood beside me.

“Do not attempt to interact,” he said.

“I know how a Pensieve works.”

“Humor me.”

“Rare request.”

His mouth tightened.

I touched the surface.

The world tipped.

I landed in a narrow lane under a gray sky.

Spinner's End.

A boy stood near a hedge.

Thin. Black-haired. Clothes too large. Watching two girls through the leaves.

I knew who he was before I saw his face.

Young Severus.

The memory did not move like a story. It moved like truth remembered: angles too sharp, sounds too clear in some places and blurred in others.

Lily laughed.

Petunia complained.

Severus watched.

I felt the adult Snape beside me but did not look at him.

The boy was lonely enough to make my throat hurt.

He was also rude.

That mattered.

When he finally spoke to Lily, he was eager and awkward and too intense. He told her about magic like a secret he had been waiting his whole life to give someone. He insulted Petunia when she mocked him. Lily defended her sister.

The boy's face closed.

Even then.

Walls in miniature.

The memory shifted.

Hogwarts Express.

A compartment.

James Potter and Sirius Black.

Names I knew from history became children in front of me.

Cruel jokes.

House loyalties claimed before anyone understood what they would cost.

Severus's anger came quick.

So did theirs.

Lily tried to keep peace.

The memory shifted again.

Older now.

A corridor.

Lily furious.

Severus trying to apologize for a word he had called her.

Not a small word.

Not an accident stripped of context.

A slur spoken in humiliation and anger, backed by friends who used it easily.

“I didn't mean you,” the boy insisted.

Lily's face changed.

I felt something twist inside me.

Because there it was.

The terrible logic of prejudice: not you, as if affection for one person repaired contempt for everyone like them.

Lily refused it.

Good.

I was glad she did.

Beside me, adult Snape did not move.

The memory shifted.

A hill.

Dumbledore.

Rain.

A young man with panic in his face, begging for Lily's life after learning the prophecy he had carried was being used against her family.

He did not ask for James first.

He did not ask for Harry first.

The ugliness of that was there.

So was the desperation.

Dumbledore's disgust.

Snape's willingness to trade anything for her safety.

Then another shift.

A room after her death.

Snape broken in a way I had never seen him.

Dumbledore demanding what he would do now.

The memory ended before the answer.

I rose from the Pensieve gasping.

The office returned.

Snape stood near the window with his back to me.

I gripped the edge of the table until the dizziness passed.

Neither of us spoke.

At last I said, “Why that memory?”

“Those memories.”

“You know what I mean.”

His shoulders tightened.

“Because people will tell you a cleaner version.”

I waited.

“Potter will tell you I loved Lily. Minerva will tell you I spied for Dumbledore. The Ministry may decide those facts weigh against others.”

He turned.

“I wanted you to see what the phrase loved Lily can conceal.”

His face was controlled, but his hands were clenched.

“The prejudice,” I said.

“Yes.”

“The slur.”

“Yes.”

“The fact that your first concern was her.”

“Yes.”

“Not James. Not Harry.”

“Yes.”

Each answer cost him.

I did not rescue him.

“That was wrong,” I said.

His face tightened.

“Yes.”

“And you changed later.”

“Yes.”

“Both.”

A breath.

“Yes.”

I looked back at the Pensieve.

“I don't pity that boy.”

Snape flinched.

“I feel sorry for him,” I continued. “That's different.”

His eyes narrowed.

“He was lonely. Poor. bullied. angry. He found people who offered belonging and fed the worst parts of him. I am sorry that happened to him.”

I met Snape's gaze.

“And he still hurt Lily. He still chose people who hurt others. Pain did not make those choices inevitable.”

“No.”

“You agree.”

“Of course I agree.”

“Then why do you look like you're waiting for me to leave?”

The question cut through the room.

Snape froze.

I could see the answer before he spoke.

Because I had seen it.

Because he had handed me the ugliest version and expected disgust to complete the ritual.

“I have no intention of leaving because you were an awful sixteen-year-old,” I said.

His mouth twitched despite everything.

“I was awful at seventeen as well.”

“Thank you for the correction.”

“And twenty.”

“Stop showing off.”

That got a real, brief laugh.

Then his expression broke again.

“You should be disgusted.”

“I am disgusted by some of what I saw.”

His face went still.

“I am not disgusted by your existence.”

Silence.

I stepped closer.

Not touching.

“Those are not the same thing.”

Snape looked down.

For a long moment, I thought he would retreat.

Instead he held out his hand.

I took it.

His grip was tight.

“Thank you,” I said.

“For what?”

“For trusting me with something that did not make you look good.”

His gaze lifted.

“That is a strange thing to thank someone for.”

“It's a strange thing to offer.”

“Perhaps.”

We stood beside the Pensieve until the silver surface became still.

Before we left, Snape took the vial back.

He held it up to the light.

“I may not use it at the hearing.”

“That's your choice.”

“They may require corroboration.”

“Then you decide what is necessary.”

His eyes moved toward me.

“You are not going to tell me what is strategically best?”

“Not about this.”

Another small surprise.

He pocketed the memory.

At the door, he paused.

“I did mean one thing,” he said.

“What?”

“When I was a child. I meant it when I told her she was a witch.”

I remembered the eager boy, offering magic like a door out of the gray world.

“I know.”

Snape nodded.

I thought about the memory for days afterward.

Not because I wanted more of it.

Because receiving it had changed the shape of consent between us.

Severus had spent much of his life having privacy invaded in one direction or another: Legilimency, surveillance, blackmail, school gossip, wartime secrets dragged into public judgment. Offering a memory was not the same as surrendering the right to keep others.

So when I caught myself forming a question about Lily's final year at school, I stopped.

He noticed.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“That is transparently false.”

“I had a question. Then I decided it wasn't mine.”

His eyes stayed on me.

“You may ask.”

“That's not the same as you wanting to answer.”

A long pause.

“No,” he said. “It is not.”

He returned to the inventory sheet.

Ten minutes later, without looking up, he told me a completely unrelated story about Lily once hexing a boy who had thrown mud at her sister.

I laughed.

He did too, quietly.

That was how I learned the difference between information extracted and memory shared.

We walked back to the dungeon together.

prose_fingerprint: emotionally direct without flattening emotion into exposition
ground abstract feelings in concrete physical details, objects, weather, rooms, gestures, and sensory anchors
alternate compact emotional beats with fuller reflective paragraphs
let dialogue carry relationship pressure while narration carries interior consequence
use humor and ordinary practical actions to make vulnerable scenes feel lived-in rather than staged
favor character-specific reactions and small remembered details over generic declarations
allow grief, identity, survival, belonging, home, change, vulnerability, care, and autonomy to recur as thematic pressure
end scenes or chapters on an emotional consequence, changed understanding, concrete image, callback, or forward pull
preserve first-person immediacy and avoid omniscient knowledge outside Jasper's perception
use semicolons selectively for linked thoughts rather than mechanically
dialogue_fingerprint: continuous dialogue should sound conversational rather than like alternating speeches
interrupt dialogue with gestures, environment, hesitation, humor, and internal reaction
let characters dodge, misunderstand, tease, repair, and return to earlier wording
do not make every character equally eloquent, equally dominant, or equally emotionally transparent
relationship_fingerprint: slow burn must accumulate evidence: remembered preferences, repaired conflict, shared routines, private jokes, and practical care
attraction should not erase plot, outside obligations, individual goals, or conflict
vulnerability is strongest when it changes later behavior
after an intense/private interlude, resume with reconnection, humor, care, consequences, memory updates, and the next plot beat rather than treating intimacy as a reset
